lines.text: Welcome! Let's build your first network together, one step at a time. Tip: rest your mouse on any button to see what it does. Click Next to begin.
Let's get a closer look first. Zoom in on the play area: scroll your mouse wheel, or click the zoom-in button in the bottom-right corner.
You can also pan the camera around. Try it — hold <key>WASD</key> to move the view.
You can also turn the view to see things from another side. Click a turn button in the bottom-right corner (or press <key>Q</key> / <key>E</key>).
Every device needs somewhere to sit. Click Table, then click the glowing circle once to set the table's first corner.
First corner set! Now move your mouse to the new glowing circle — the table stretches to follow — and click once more to set the opposite corner.
Tables can be resized. Click your table once to select it.
Handles appeared on its corners and edges. Press and hold the marked edge handle.
Keep holding, drag the edge out to the glowing circle, then let go to make the table bigger.
Press and hold PC, drag it over the table, then let go to drop it there. It must land inside the table's glowing outline.
Now rotate it: left-click your PC to select it (it glows cyan), then click a rotate button at the bottom of the screen. (Holding <key>R</key> and scrolling works too.)
Placed devices can be moved too. Click and hold your PC to pick it up.
Keep holding, drag it to the glowing spot, then let go to place it down.
Drag another PC from the sidebar onto the table.
That button holds more than PCs. Click the arrow beside it to see the other tools. (Right-clicking the button works too.)
Now drag Switch out onto the table — it's what connects your PCs together.
Every device has one or more ports — the small connection points cables plug into. If a device has more than one, a popup will ask which one to use when you connect a cable.
Click Cable to start wiring your network.
Now click your first PC — that's where the cable starts.
A list of free ports pops up — click one (like eth0) to plug the cable in there.
Now click the Switch to finish the connection.
Pick a free port on the Switch the same way to complete the cable.
Click Cable again, then repeat: click your second PC, pick a port, click the Switch, and pick a port there too.
Your network is built! Networks change too — let's learn to undo some of it. Click Remove, then click one of your cables to delete it.
Remove has an arrow too. Click the arrow to see the other removal tools.
Click Remove Device, then click one of your devices to delete it.
Click the arrow beside Remove again to find the last tool.
Click Remove Table, then click your table to delete it.
Great work — you've learned to build a network, and take it apart when you need to.
Right-click a PC to open its address popup, then give it an IP address and subnet mask (e.g. 192.168.1.10 / 255.255.255.0).
Right-click the other PC and give it an IP on a DIFFERENT subnet (different network portion, e.g. 192.168.2.11) — let's see what happens when two devices can't reach each other.
Click Ping, then pick the two PCs — since they're on different subnets, the ping will fail. Watch what that failure looks like.
Right-click the second PC again and change its address so it's on the SAME subnet as the first PC (e.g. 192.168.1.11).
Click Ping again — now that both PCs share a subnet, they should reach each other.
Right-click the Router to open its command line.

Type enable (or click it in the Commands list and press Run) to enter Privileged EXEC mode. Most commands are locked until you do — it's how a real router keeps casual users from breaking its config. (Tip: rest your mouse on any command to see what it does.)
Type configure terminal to enter Global Config — settings you make here apply to the whole router. A single port's own settings live one level deeper, inside Interface Config.
Type interface eth0 to configure the first port. (Tip: press Tab to auto-complete, or click the command in the Commands list.)
Type end to jump back to Privileged EXEC. You've now walked the whole map: User EXEC → Privileged EXEC → Global Config → Interface Config.
Checkpoint — no outlines this time. You're back in Privileged EXEC — get the Router into interface eth1's configuration mode on your own.
Place a Router to bridge the two subnets you're about to create.
Your Router has to be wired into both subnets before it can bridge them. Click Cable to start the first connection.
One subnet wired! Click Cable again for the second — this time from the Router to the other Switch.
Click the Router — that's where this cable starts.
Its free ports pop up — click one (like eth{n}) to plug the cable into the {device}.
That {device} has no free port left. Click an empty spot to close its list, then click the glowing {expected} instead.
Now pick a free port on the {device} the same way to complete the cable.
Now click the Router to finish the connection.
Now click the glowing Switch to finish the connection.
Now click a Switch to finish the connection.
Right-click the Router to open its CLI. Type interface eth{n}, then ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0 and no shutdown to set up your first subnet.
Now set up the second subnet: interface eth{n}, then ip address 192.168.2.1 255.255.255.0 and no shutdown — a different subnet than the first interface.
Every PC only knows how to reach devices on its own subnet directly — same network address, same mask. Anything outside that subnet is unreachable on its own.
That's what a default gateway is for: a router interface sitting on the PC's own subnet, responsible for forwarding traffic bound for anywhere else.

The Router interfaces you just configured are the gateways for their subnets. When you address each PC next, its mask decides what's "local" — everything else quietly routes through the Router instead.

Concretely: interface eth{a} → ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0 made 192.168.1.1 the gateway for that subnet — address a PC there like 192.168.1.10 255.255.255.0. Same for eth{b}: 192.168.2.1 is the gateway for a PC addressed like 192.168.2.10 255.255.255.0.

lines.text: Concretely: the ip address command you ran on each interface is exactly what made it a gateway — that same address is what you'll enter as each PC's gateway next.
Right-click a PC to open its address popup, then give the two PCs IPs matching the Router's two subnets — one PC on 192.168.1.x (eth{a}), the other on 192.168.2.x (eth{b}).
Click Ping, then pick the two PCs to confirm they can reach each other through the Router.

Click Send Packet, choose a type, then click the two PCs. HTTP Request is instant; File Transfer carries a bigger, slower payload. Press Enter to commit, then click Run Network to send real data across the Router.
So far, every subnet you've made has used the same size mask for every department — one /24 each, no matter how many hosts it actually needed.
This time, all three departments have to share ONE block: 192.168.1.0/24. You'll carve it into three pieces instead of getting a fresh block each.

Each department needs a different amount of room — one needs space for 4 hosts, one for 14, one for 30. Giving all three an identical mask would either waste addresses or not fit — that's what VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Masking) solves: sizing each piece to fit what it's actually for.
Pick a mask for each department that's big enough for its own requirement, keep all three inside that one /24, and make sure none of their address ranges overlap.

That second click landed on (or right next to) your first one, so the table would be too small to hold anything.

Click a corner further away to size it — two separate clicks, not a double-click.
